html:
A Roman aqueduct about 91 km long, the longest of the eleven that supplied ancient Rome. It was built from 144 to 140 BCE by the praetor Quintus Marcius Rex.

The money came from the spoils of 146 BCE, when Rome destroyed Carthage and Corinth. The water came from springs in the hills east of the city and ran mostly underground, but over the last stretch it crossed the plain on long arcades of stone arches. It was the first aqueduct to bring water up to the Capitoline Hill.

Romans prized its water. Pliny the Elder called it the coldest and purest of all. Later rulers, among them Agrippa and Augustus, repaired it, and Frontinus counts it among the city's great aqueducts alongside the later Aqua Claudia.

Its arches can still be seen outside Rome, and the Acqua Felice, built by Pope Sixtus V in 1586, follows much of its route.
sum: A Roman aqueduct about 91 km long, the longest of the eleven that supplied ancient Rome. It was built from 144 to 140 BCE by the praetor Quintus Marcius Rex.
